We have developed a novel method to incorporate the non-abelian aether term into a gauge theory, and applied it to a SU(2) Yang-Mills theory in different dimensions. In this process, the non-abelian aether term affects the Lagrangian, and consequently, the Stefan-Boltzmann law, Casimir energy, and Hawking temperature in ways specific to the aether term. Our results show that the aether term can significantly impact the properties of gauge fields, particularly in low-dimensional systems.

We suggest a unified model that considers both syntax and semantics, observing that
the interconnection between these two aspects is not just a theoretical idea but also
a practical one that can be leveraged in NLP tasks. Our research shows that a joint model
exhibits consistent patterns in multiple languages, exists on a continuum of formality,
and is more efficient and effective than separate models in understanding text.

Mergers of compact objects produce radioactively powered transients with a wide range of luminosity peaks, from $10^{39}$ to $10^{42}$ ergs per second. These transients, characterized by a delayed radioactivity and rapid early decay, are observed across various mass ranges. Theoretical models suggest that these events originate from the collision of neutron stars, black holes, and a range of white dwarf masses. The research focuses on these radioactively driven transients, highlighting how they can be used to study various astrophysical processes, including the formation of compact objects, the evolution of binary systems, and the synthesis of heavy elements.

We analyzed a large collection of nearby early-type galaxies from the SDSS-III/Mazurkewicz database, which includes optical spectra and photometry. Our research focused on understanding how morphological types and other properties of these galaxies vary with redshift and other factors. We found that a significant majority of these galaxies have elliptical shapes, while the remaining are lenticular galaxies. Interestingly, we observed an increase in the fraction of tidal features as the stellar mass of these galaxies increases. Our research also revealed that the tidal features are more prevalent in galaxies with higher fractions of old metal-poor stars. Furthermore, we found that the tidal features are more prevalent in galaxies located in dense clusters and groups, which may be attributed to the effects of environmental factors. Our research provides new insights into the formation and evolution of early-type galaxies and their interactions with their surroundings.

We present a new theory of gravitation, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, which offers a groundbreaking solution to the Radiation Problem in massive star formation. This theory, based on an innovative concept, enables the radiation of a significant amount of energy from a star's surface, preventing the star from becoming excessively luminous and massive during its early stages of development. The new theory, unlike Einstein's General Relativity, predicts a unique and specific relationship between the gravitational constant and fundamental physical constants, which can be experimentally verified.

A FRB, specifically FRB 20201124A, has been observed in 2021 by the Jansky VLA and the MWA, revealing an FRB burst and a coincident optical event approximately 1.5 months apart. This event, detected by the TESS and the NTT, marks the first time an FRB burst and a concurrent optical event, associated with the same source, have been observed within such a short time frame. This discovery significantly constrains various FRB emission models, particularly those that predict optical emission to occur alongside radio emission. The TESS and the NTT observations of the event 1.5 months apart also impose new constraints on the population of FRB afterglows and on the energy budget of the event itself.

The precise modeling of CPA and NLO-based laser systems is a complex task,
requiring a deep understanding of the chirp dynamics within the different system
components. We develop a unified model to describe the evolution of the laser
field spectrum as a function of its mean frequency, mean bandwidth, and
central frequency location. This model accounts for CPA systems featuring
dispersive compensation, various types of amplifiers, and various modulation
methods, as well as NLO systems involving modulation in the absence of a filter
and modulation combined with a subsequent removal of the blue wing.

This paper introduces a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework called MAGIC, aimed at training a decoder that generates text that is both contextually coherent and image-driven. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on pre-trained models, we formulate the text generation process as a sequential decision-making problem where each word is a state-action pair. The proposed framework combines two key objectives: a contextual coherence objective to maintain consistency with the conversation history and an attention-based objective to connect generated text to visual cues. By addressing these objectives simultaneously, we achieve a seamless integration of visual and language models and obtain superior results on multiple benchmarks for art description and multi-modal task generation.

The Monero Delegated RingCT, a groundbreaking privacy-preserving signature protocol, enables fast and scalable verification of unforgeable cryptographic signatures. This work presents an in-depth, practical guide to implementing Delegated RingCT, allowing for the batch verification of hundreds of thousands of signatures per second while also reducing verification time to under 10 milliseconds on a single CPU. A working code implementation is provided for the Delegated RingCT, incorporating complete Haskell code with detailed comments for easy understanding. The verification process is broken down into complex, high-level cryptographic primitives, with the support of the user-friendly Haskell programming language, making the code highly readable and accessible. The level of the code is production-ready, and it is being actively maintained.

A novel method for measuring the beam-beam closed orbit difference with a high degree of precision has been developed. This method relies on measuring the differences between the closed orbits of colliding beams, which can directly quantify the beam-beam effect and its impact on the beam's trajectory. Observing the beam-induced shift in a localized region allows for a calculation of the beam-beam gradient, providing further insight into the phenomenon. Researchers have successfully applied this method in the LHC, where measurements of beam-beam closed orbit differences and beam-induced shifts around the Interaction Point 1 have been made, and the observed values are consistent with theoretical predictions.

Machine learning has gained significant attention in modeling the complex behavior of solid materials. One of the key challenges in solid mechanics is capturing history-dependent plasticity, which heavily relies on accurate plastic strain predictions. To address this challenge, a novel continuum damage-plasticity model was developed using a neural network in three stages. The proposed model utilizes neural networks to model the intricate relationship between plastic strain and stress state, thereby improving the accuracy of history-dependent plasticity modeling. To prevent overfitting in multi-task learning, the neural network was trained to adapt to various stress states. Furthermore, to leverage past learning and reduce training costs, the model can benefit from continual learning without forgetting previous knowledge. To achieve this, the backpropagation through time method was employed to help the model understand the relationship between stress and plastic strain at different time steps. The results indicate that the proposed model can effectively capture the complex behavior of concrete under compression, surpassing traditional models.

A recent study has generated significant controversy due to its unconventional explanation for the $\epsilon(10753)$ state, which is now addressed by an alternative model. A more conventional approach, based on the assumption that $\epsilon(10753)$ is a $1^{3}D_{1}$ state, resolves the issues raised by the new report. Furthermore, this analysis reveals that the $D^{(*)}S^{(*)}$ production rates in the decay of $\epsilon(10753)$ are in line with the predictions derived from a perturbative QCD framework.

We investigate quantized stochastic gradient descent in the context of training deep neural networks, focusing on the trade-off between model accuracy and bit allocation for weights and gradients. We introduce AskewSGD, a new approach that achieves better performance compared to existing methods, including SGD with quantized gradients and even 16-bit SGD. AskewSGD optimizes the balance between model accuracy and data compression by assigning 1 bit to weights and gradients equally, allowing for a significant reduction in data transmission. We evaluate AskewSGD on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets using resnet models, achieving state-of-the-art results, especially in the limited 1-bit communication setting.

As a result of advancements in 3D printing and the development of innovative materials, researchers have made significant progress in designing and creating robots with the ability to mimic the unique characteristics of invertebrate and vertebrate animals' appendages. These robots, classified as soft robots, exhibit greater flexibility than traditional mechanical systems. However, existing soft robot designs do not accurately replicate the flexure of living creatures' limbs. Our study aims to bridge this gap by introducing a new continuum robot design that can be used in environments with unpredictable obstacles. The design features an external structure composed of inextensible elements that can be bent using pneumatic pressure, similar to the way animal muscles contract. Notably, the design mimics the flexure of a living creature's limb by incorporating the ability to contract and expand. Our experiments demonstrate that the new design surpasses conventional robots with continuous surfaces in terms of its ability to bend and conform to obstacles.

The Jacobi group, specifically Je(2;R), is not Hermitian-admissible, yet we have adapted a method to introduce left-invariant metrics that can be extended to the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane U(n,n+1;R) x T, where T represents the T-action. We have demonstrated that these metrics correspond to the left translation of the Kähler balanced metric on the Siegel upper half-plane U(n) x T, and they also correspond to the left translation of the left-invariant Kähler metric on the Siegel upper half-plane U(n). Furthermore, we have shown that the left-invariant Kähler metric on Je(2;R) satisfies the strong Kähler cyclic condition, and it also possesses a left-invariant Kähler form ω that satisfies dω = -θ(θ) for positive constants c.

Recent advances in fact verification have led to impressive performance, but the complexity of language poses a significant challenge for model effectiveness. To overcome this limitation, we propose FAV, a fact verification model that leverages the decomposition of complex statements into simpler components for enhanced performance. FUV employs a sentence decomposition model to break down input statements into their constituent parts and uses a knowledge graph to represent relationships between those components. By combining graph-based reasoning with language models, FAV can accurately verify the truthfulness of complex statements with decomposition. Through comprehensive evaluations on Complex UMTS and Fever datasets, FAV achieves superior performance, outdoing existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study presents a cutting-edge approach that empowers generative models to create high-quality outputs without being limited by the availability of labeled data. The researchers' method builds upon the established principles of contrastive learning, incorporating a unique twist that significantly enhances the quality of generated outputs. The framework's versatility is demonstrated through the successful application to multiple generative tasks, including image editing, image creation, and language modeling. The outcomes of these experiments showcase a notable improvement, with our approach surpassing existing methods in several key metrics.

We've modified the hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling algorithms to sample directly from the posterior distribution without relying on Hastings ratios found in Metropolis-Hastings sampling. The modifications lead to improved efficiency compared to traditional hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling, as demonstrated by the new posterior coupling efficiency of the method. The new approach, combining hit-and-run and slice sampling, offers a significant improvement in performance compared to its individual components, achieving a 2.5-3.0 times efficiency boost in various Bayesian inference scenarios.

In the realm of graph theory and computer science, finding the shortest path between two points is a crucial task. To expedite this process, researchers have developed algorithms that pre-calculate and store "distance labels" for all vertices, allowing for faster distance calculations. This paper focuses on enhancing the efficiency of these pre-stored distance labels in fault-prone graphs, where one vertex may fail during a distance calculation. To this end, the concepts of optimal and $\epsilon$-optimal fault-tolerant distance labels are introduced and their properties, such as size and runtime, are investigated. Interestingly, the research reveals that while optimal fault-tolerant distance labels are not possible for all graphs, they can be approximated with an arbitrarily small loss in size. Furthermore, the study highlights the connection between these labels and other areas, such as the set cover problem and the creation of compact hypergraphs.

In a one-dimensional driven Bose-Hubbard model with dissipation, a continuous phase transition occurs that can be explored using spatial correlations within a gas of bosons. By examining these correlations through their Fourier transforms, researchers have found that their Gaussian form provides insight into the transition's control parameters. The non-extensive nature of the correlations manifests itself in the Fourier-transformed data, which peaks at zero momentum and conforms to a Gaussian curve. By fitting a Gaussian model, scientists can map out the transition line in the driving and dissipation parameter space.

Let M denote a complete Riemannian manifold with no boundary. Consider F as a uniformly convex closed cone within the space of symmetric 2×2 matrices. In a bounded domain Ω⊂M^2, we define L as a linear elliptic operator within the conespace F. We establish that the Dirichlet problem for linear elliptic equations within the conespace F can be solved in a particular type of domain called a poly-convex one. Additionally, we derive a gradient estimate for these equations.

A novel approach to automatic brain tissue segmentation in MRI images utilizes a combination of 3D and 2D Gaussian Processes. This method generates probabilistic estimates of tissue types and their gradients within each voxel, utilizing 3D and 2D information. By incorporating prior knowledge about tissue distribution patterns, our technique achieves accurate segmentation of brain tissues. We demonstrate its effectiveness through evaluations on synthetic data and a public MRI dataset, comparing our results to those of state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms.

Our research explores the dynamics of interplay between thermal decay and nonthermal growth in a system of intermediately interacting Bosons that are damped and then accelerated by an external driving force. We utilize a method that combines the 1D Gross-Pitaevskii model with input-output theory to investigate thermal decay in the time domain. We find that thermal decay is significantly hindered by heating caused by the changing drive, which results in the emergence of a nonthermal phase where Bose condensation can occur. This phase transition is influenced by the rate of driving and can be observed in real experiments with ultracold gases.

We show that for a sequence of strictly convex functions $u_\epsilon$ in the unit cube in 3D, where each $u_\epsilon$ satisfies a specific convexity inequality, it can be proven that in the weak-$W^{1,\infty}$ sense the sequence converges to a limit $D^2p_\epsilon$ converging to a convex function $p$ in the weak-$W^{1,p}$ sense, provided $p$ is less than 3, and the $u_\epsilon$ converge uniformly to a convex function $p$ while its gradient converges weakly to a symmetric matrix $A$ which is also the Hessian of $p$. This implies a specific limit behavior of $u_\epsilon$ which is a direct result of a new W^{1,p} compactness theorem for a class of strictly convex functions. This is a specific instance of a more general principle discovered by the authors in 2019.

We explore the optimal configuration of an asymmetric two-level quantum system clock to maximize its precision. This system is coupled to a measurement device and a probe field, with the measurement device's outcome influencing the clock's accuracy. Our analysis reveals that the measurement noise reduction can be leveraged to enhance the clock's accuracy, with this improvement being most pronounced at low frequencies. Additionally, we found that the measurement can only slightly improve the clock's accuracy in comparison to its accuracy without the measurement influence, with this improvement being of the order of $\epsilon^2$. We also investigated how the measurement influence scales with the number of photons in the probe field, with the measurement influence on the clock's accuracy being negligible for large probe fields.

This study tackles the challenge of optimizing energy consumption and ensuring reliability within network path planning. The research presents a novel approach called the Heuristic for Optimizing Future Energy System (HFES), which effectively minimizes the overall energy expenditure of nodes along a specific path, thereby enhancing end-to-end reliability. The approach initially divides a given path into segments based on predefined criteria, then applies an optimization technique to identify the optimal set of nodes within each segment that contribute least to energy dissipation. The HFES algorithm has been successfully tested in a real-world Internet setting, demonstrating a 10% reduction in average energy consumption and a 15% improvement in end-to-end reliability.

The majority of state-of-the-art image retrieval models heavily rely on the
perception of a global negative sampling strategy, which is often criticized for
its lack of efficiency. In this paper, we present a novel image retrieval
framework called Pairwise Loss Gradient Analysis (PLGA), which reveals and
exploits a crucial property of pairwise loss gradients that significantly
improves feature representation for image retrieval. Specifically, we identify
two key components within these gradients: a discriminative part that creates
distinct features for different classes, and a diversity part that generates
diverse features within the same class. By analyzing and controlling these
gradients, we effectively prevent the model from falling into local optima,
thereby achieving improved feature representation and better image retrieval
performance. Our approach, which only requires a single forward pass and one
backward pass, achieves state-of-the-art results on a variety of benchmark
datasets, including ImageNet, Google ImageNet, and COCO, with a performance
boost of up to 10.0% and a large margin, all while maintaining a low
computational cost.

We examine the inherent structural limitations imposed by an erasure correction code composed of a singular tensor type. This is achieved by converting the standard tensor contraction into a matrix product operator code and applying a channel that erases tensors. We find that if the tensor network code consists of one tensor type, certain inequalities must hold, which in a classical context corresponds to a probability vector satisfying specific inequalities. We also establish a connection between the original problem and an optimization problem, enabling us to identify key properties of the tensor that are critical for the code's functionality. Notably, we identify tensors that meet the imposed constraints, are contractible for any number of erasures, and are maximal in this context. Additionally, we identify tensors that are nearly maximal, failing to correct only a single erasure.

The origin of magnetized radio filaments in star-forming galaxies is still unclear,
despite their presence in a range of galaxies. We present the first results of a
study of these radio filaments in the nearby galaxy M83 using the MWA radio
array. We identify a network of radio filaments in M83 that are associated with
a series of radio hotspots. We propose two possible origins for the observed
filaments: (1) they form due to the interaction between the central radio source
and the surrounding hotspots, or (2) they form due to the gravitational
instability of magnetized gas in the galaxy's disk. We discuss the implications of
these findings for understanding the formation of radio filaments in nearby
galaxies.

Controlling large groups of distributed energy resources with distributed control methods is highly effective due to its simplicity and scalability. This paper examines two prevalent leader-follower control approaches, which enable a central controller to set a specific resource's operation while other devices automatically respond to changes in that operation. We initially examine the stability of a class of control systems that utilize these methods, focusing on controllers that combine first-order dynamics with leading and following behavior. We develop two fundamental conditions that ensure the stability of a specific equilibrium under specific circumstances. To apply these conditions, we create a procedure to adjust the feedback parameters in a way that guarantees the stability of the adjusted system at the desired equilibrium. We validate our theoretical findings through simulations of a microgrid that controls its inverters to set the frequency and reactive power levels.

This research presents a regret analysis for a delayed and potentially corrupted version of the multi-armed bandit problem, where all arm rewards are generated from independent and identically distributed Bernoulli distributions. A new regret bound is derived, dependent on the delay and corruption rates of the best arm's rewards as well as the suboptimal arm's best rewards, all treated as arbitrary functions. The analysis demonstrates that the rate of regret is directly influenced by how often the best arm's rewards are missed or delayed, underscoring the critical role these factors play in minimizing regret. The findings are validated through a specific case study involving a linearly increasing delay and a zero corruption rate, offering an alternative proof for a previously established regret regret bound in the delay and corruption-free setting.

We present a text-generation framework for dialogue that fulfills two main objectives. Firstly, it seeks to address the text-generation field by offering a more structured and methodical approach, moving away from the current reliance on recurrent neural networks and long-term memory. Our new model excels in being more efficient and versatile, while also producing text that is more natural and in line with dialogue history. Secondly, we propose a novel and underlying theory for dialogue text-generation, allowing us to break down text generation into comprehensible and learnable concepts. This theory enables us to identify the underlying principles that drive text generation and to assign corresponding values to those principles.

Quantum chromodynamics, formulated in the late 1960s, has since been explored 
extensively, particularly regarding the characteristics of strong-interaction matter.
A key area of research involves the application of lattice field theory through 
Monte Carlo simulations. The theoretical framework is well-established, yet the 
associated simulations are computationally demanding and intricate. This review 
synthesizes recent research on the properties of confined quarks and gluons.
A new area of exploration, the "deconfined" state of matter, is also discussed.
The matter described by QCD at extreme energy density and temperature holds 
significance in the context of heavy-ion collisions and the early universe.
Recent research on the deconfined state of matter in the quark-gluon plasma is 
covered, along with the associated theoretical and experimental developments.
The review also examines ongoing research involving neutron stars and the 
associated matter properties.

The variability of stochastic processes, such as ocean currents and wind, poses significant challenges to understanding the dynamics of offshore wind turbines. These dynamic systems are heavily influenced by the interplay of complex factors, including turbulence and irregular waves. To investigate the effects of stochasticity on the structural loads of offshore wind turbines, we've developed a new approach to modeling the dynamics of these systems. This method relies on a technique for sampling the joint probability distributions of the turbulent states within these systems, allowing us to examine the effects of turbulence on the dynamic response of the turbines. Our results indicate that stochasticity can have a profound impact on the structural loads experienced by offshore wind turbines, with the effects of turbulence being particularly significant.

This research aims to utilize social media data to identify the geographic area of a disaster and assess the public sentiment in surrounding regions. By analyzing tweets related to a specific disaster, we aim to discover the type of disaster that occurred, map the emotional landscape of the public in different geographic areas, and discover any underlying connections between emotional responses and geographic locations. To achieve this, we have developed a novel framework that integrates a social media data visualization tool with geospatial sentiment visualization, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of the disaster's impact on the public. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in identifying the disaster's geographic footprint and emotional patterns of the public.

We define the absolute nilpotency degree of a group as the smallest exponent r such that the product of r+1 commutators equals the identity element in every normal subgroup of the group. This concept is an alternative to the classical nilpotency degree and is more informative and less restrictive. We demonstrate that the absolute nilpotency degree can be used to determine the boundedness of the torsion coefficients of the Schur multiplier in infinite groups. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the absolute nilpotency degree and other group invariants, such as the exponent of the commutator subgroup, the exponent of the Frattini subgroup, and the exponent of the commutator functor applied to a group. We also examine the effect of the absolute nilpotency degree on the boundedness of the Schur multiplier's torsion coefficients in specific classes of groups, including D-groups and B-groups.

A new approach to deconvolving spectral changes resulting from intense, short-duration laser exposure is introduced. This addresses the challenge of ill-posedness in tackling experimental data, particularly when dealing with noise. A key feature of this approach is its ability to utilize a single, smooth function to describe the modified spectral propagation operator, thereby reducing complexity. This strategy enables the reconstruction of operator eigenfunctions and their associated eigenvalues. The proposed method is demonstrated through simulations and experiments, including a study on the dissociation of iodine molecules and an examination of how the pulse duration affects the observed spectral changes. Additionally, the effectiveness of this strategy in handling noisy data is highlighted.

This study presents a comprehensive approach for assessing the reliability of object detection systems within autonomous vehicles. A Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) tracker is incorporated to effectively follow multiple targets in a simulated vehicle's environment. A novel metric called Probabilistic Association Confidence (PAC) is developed to measure tracking accuracy. Additionally, a novel metric called Average Detection Accuracy (ADA) is proposed to gauge overall system performance. These metrics are applied to an autonomous vehicle navigating through various obstacles in a dynamic setting.

In this research, we explore holographic duals for interface conformal field theory (iCFT) within AdS$_3$ spacetime. Utilizing gHRT surfaces, we reveal how the reflected entropy exhibits universal patterns, specifically the Markov gap, for certain configurations. Furthermore, we develop and apply reconstruction regions for scalar operators in iCFT through the use of replica trick methods.

In this research, a novel extreme learning machine (ELM) variant is proposed for channel estimation in systems with repeated symbol sequences, where the transmission time is shorter than the delay spread of the channel and conventional methods are ineffective. The proposed ELM variant addresses limitations of conventional techniques and imperfect hardware by incorporating an $L_1$-norm regularizer, demonstrating superior performance compared to conventional and conventional+Tikhonov methods through simulation outcomes.

In the context of quantum mechanics, it is often assumed that measurements are exclusively projective. However, we demonstrate that non-projective measurements can be recast as projective ones, yielding identical outcomes. This is only feasible in the absence of decoherence. We also show that non-unitary operations, such as those performed by quantum cloners, can be formulated as projective measurements coupled with an auxiliary system. These novel measurement definitions enable the formulation of novel theorems, for instance, a non-projective version of von Neumann's statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics.

G2-instantons are known to exhibit rigidity when they appear in solutions of the equations that define G2-instantons. The researchers proved that instantons with abelian properties are rigid within the space of all G2-instanton solutions, provided the space is compact. Furthermore, they found that certain non-abelian G2-instantons can also be rigid if the space is compact. To arrive at these findings, the team relied on a differentiable version of a mathematical concept that they developed, which they call the generalized Calabi-Yau threefold.

The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of contact tracing technologies, but the implementation of these tools raises significant privacy concerns, particularly the potential for government-led mass surveillance. This paper investigates how the government can exploit contact tracing systems to monitor citizens' activities, and proposes a strategy for which CT features should be safeguarded to prevent government surveillance.

A new approach has been developed to examine the behavior of entangled quantum systems in the presence of decoherence, which is rooted in the principles of symmetries and co-invariance. This method effectively captures the interplay between decoherence, the formation of entanglement, and the separation of quantum subsystems. To test this theory, we have applied it to the dynamics of the Bell state under dephasing in the Jaynes-Cummings model, the interaction of two coherent states with opposite components, and the entanglement of two pairs of qubits subjected to local decoherence. To further explore co-invariance, we have investigated the interaction of two pairs of qubits with opposite entanglement types, finding that local decoherence impacts them differently. To model decoherence, we have treated each qubit as an independent two-level system interacting with an independent environment of spinless particles. To gain a deeper understanding of co-invariance, we have analyzed an isolated system of four qubits from the perspective of co-invariant bases. This work lays the groundwork for future research into the general case of multi-particle environments and the entanglement of systems with distinct numbers of qubits.

We suggest that verifying high-level code using proof obligations is challenging due to the lack of concrete meaning for abstract language elements. To address this, we explore translating high-level features into a lower-level language, which is used as a reference for verification, thereby simplifying the process by relying on a well-established semantics for the target language. This approach is demonstrated through the verification of a subset of Java, which is being adapted to a functional version of x86 assembly code, called X86FL, that enforces functional principles. To ensure the correctness of the translation, we provide type and termination restrictions along with a formal method for generating verification evidence. We also present case studies that illustrate the benefits of this technique, which include the verification of a Java hash map, which was previously difficult to verify, and the verification of a high-level algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor.

I. salicifolium, a previously unclassified Iochroma species native to the Andean foothills in Ecuador, has been the subject of this study. The overall goal of the research is to enhance the understanding of the Iochroma genus' taxonomy and phylogeny. The main objective of the investigation is to examine the phylogeny of I. salicifolium and confirm its status as a distinct species. The approach taken in the research involves the use of both nuclear and plastid DNA sequences to analyze the phylogeny of the species. The results of the analysis indicate that I. salicifolium is distinct from its closest relatives, which are a clade containing I. viridiflorum and I. viridiflorum var. andicola. The findings of the research indicate that the species is a distinct lineage and is not closely related to its closest relatives. The research also provides insights into the biogeography of the Iochroma genus and highlights the importance of the Andean foothills in the dispersal of the species. The research has significant implications for the taxonomy and phylogeny of the Iochroma genus and highlights the need for further research to fully understand the taxonomy and phylogeny of the genus.

This extension of Ramanujan's well-known identity utilizes the Hurwitz zeta function to create a more general form of an integral kernel. Furthermore, we will derive several series expansions for the Hurwitz zeta function based on this generalized identity.

We introduce a novel equivariant cohomology theory, specifically for the elliptic cohomology of torus spaces under certain conditions, and demonstrate its existence by constructing an elliptic cohomology theory that applies to algebraic varieties with torus actions in a related context.

Machine learning has become a crucial tool for modeling complex geometric data, yet the underlying principles of these methods remain unclear. In response, researchers have developed an interactive deep learning framework that integrates unsupervised learning and visualization to uncover the hidden structures in geometric data. This integration enables users to interactively explore and refine model outputs, ultimately transforming the learning process into a collaborative human-computer experience. The proposed method is demonstrated through the analysis of the Manhattan skyline geometry, showcasing its potential to reveal intricate geometric insights.

A thorough examination of the charmonium production process through a double parton collision is carried out using a specific model that incorporates the spatial distribution of partons within a proton. The analysis is performed with the aim of comparing the cross-sections for the production of $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ and investigating how the impact of the correlation parameter varies under these two scenarios. Our results show that the $\theta$-parameter $\beta$ for the production of $J/\psi + \eta_c$ is consistently lower than that observed in $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ productions, and our calculations reveal that the DPS contribution to $J/\psi + \eta_c$ production is substantial, with a lower bound of approximately 10% at a rapidity of $|Y| < 2.5$ and a transverse momentum of $p_T > 5$ GeV/c.

To ensure user account recovery and deter unauthorized access, every user account requires a PIN. Current research suggests that users' purpose-specific understanding of PIN security is a crucial factor in determining their level of concern for security. To ensure that the PIN system implemented in Signal for messaging purposes is as secure as possible, we conducted an in-depth study of Signal users in the US. Our research focused on how users perceive the purpose and security of their Signal accounts and whether their end-to-end encryption settings, including their Signal PIN, are appropriately configured. Our findings reveal that many users are unaware of their Signal account's purpose-specific nature, including the use of a Signal PIN for access protection. Furthermore, we discovered that users who do not recognize the unique features of Signal, such as the use of Signal PINs for access protection, are more likely to use weak or no PINs at all. To address this issue, we made recommendations for improving user education and awareness regarding Signal's security and privacy settings.

In certain solar energy calculations, it is beneficial to use solar-weighted quadrature rules over Gaussian quadrature rules due to their ability to closely match the solar energy distribution. However, constructing optimal solar-weighted quadrature rules with many nodes is computationally demanding. A recent approach by \cite{Goncalves2021} effectively reduces the complexity by leveraging precomputed data, but the method has its limitations in terms of accuracy and applicability. This work presents an alternative strategy to achieve similar results by combining \cite{Cools2008}'s selection of points with \cite{Muller2005}'s Kaczmarz method for solving systems of linear equations. By doing so, the quadrature rules can be built in a matter of seconds, with improved accuracy and flexibility. Our implementation in Julia is freely available on GitHub.

In many fields, including machine learning and data analysis, it's common to encounter large-scale complex networks. Computing their fundamental properties, such as eigenvalues and directional derivatives, is crucial for the development of efficient algorithms. However, these operations are computationally expensive, and their high costs can hinder the development of scalable methods. To address this issue, we introduce ViViT, a neural network designed to compute the spectral decomposition of symmetric matrices efficiently. This method allows for the rapid determination of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which can be applied in a black-box setting. By using ViViT, the computational complexity is reduced to O(N), where N represents the total number of matrix entries. This novel approach enables the fast computation of the spectral decomposition and its various applications, such as kernel methods, de-noising, and low-rank approximations. Through extensive experiments, ViViT is shown to be effective in multiple scenarios, including the computation of the spectral decomposition of the graph matrix of the Facebook social network, where it outperforms other methods by 3 orders of magnitude.

This study investigates a well-documented issue in English word representations known as grammatical gender bias, an unintended consequence of training data and language models. The research examines how removing this bias from English word embeddings impacts their quality in both native and translated language environments, focusing specifically on translated word embeddings. The findings indicate that eliminating grammatical bias from English word embeddings, derived from multiple languages, is feasible and does not compromise their quality. Furthermore, the study discovered that word embeddings from native language training data are more prone to grammatical bias than those from translated data. The researchers also highlight the need for further investigation into grammatical bias in word representations of other languages.

T. Uchiyama demonstrated that the action of a finitely generated, virtually nilpotent group on the space of its characters has a distinct, slow-growing property known as subexponential complexity. This property stands in stark contrast to the exponential complexity growth found in Lins Neto and Vianna's work on toroidal dynamics. As part of their research, Uchiyama and Balog found that any finite group action on a manifold with ergodic elements of subexponential order fails to be totally minimal. However, the total minimality of the action of a finitely generated virtually nilpotent group on the characters of its abelianization has been proven, resolving a potential discrepancy.

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the pose of objects by utilizing low-resolution input images. The method combines a lightweight convolutional neural network that predicts the pose of an object based solely on low-resolution input images, with an optimization technique that refines the estimated pose. The optimization is performed by leveraging the gradient of the loss function with respect to the pose parameters, under the assumption that the object's appearance remains unchanged. The proposed method is notably efficient in terms of both computation and data requirements, and can operate at a high frame rate. Experimental results demonstrate that the method achieves a significant improvement of up to 20% in pose estimation accuracy compared to a baseline approach, while also outperforming it in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, the method is able to estimate the pose of objects with a high degree of accuracy even when working with low-resolution input images, outdoing a baseline approach that is trained on full-resolution images by up to 25%. The method is also able to track objects with a high degree of accuracy even when working with low-resolution input sequences, outperforming a baseline approach that is trained on full-resolution sequences.

This study evaluates the potential of using big data and advanced machine learning techniques to create an efficient, accurate, and resilient system for forecasting travel times. Traffic management is a crucial component of urban planning, and accurate travel time predictions are essential for optimizing traffic flow and enhancing driver experience. Current travel time forecasting methods primarily rely on in-depth traffic knowledge and complex graph-based models. However, these methods can be resource-intensive and difficult to implement. In contrast, our research demonstrates that simple gradient-based models can achieve comparable results. We utilize traffic information from the U.S. and test different approaches, finding that big data-driven gradient boosting techniques can outperform more complex alternatives. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that data-driven methods can achieve the same accuracy as traditional approaches, but with significantly lower computational requirements. This research highlights the potential of using data-driven techniques to create an efficient and accurate traffic forecasting system, ultimately contributing to the development of next-generation traffic management systems.

Causal inference techniques are increasingly being used in machine learning to create more transparent and reliable models. This paper focuses on using causal methods to evaluate a specific concept in fairness analysis, known as counterfactual fairness. Counterfactual fairness is a classification problem-specific idea, which aims to assess whether a classification model is fair by considering hypothetical scenarios. The paper demonstrates how causal inference methods can contribute to machine learning model transparency by using causal representation learning to identify the underlying causes of data and remove their influence. This approach allows for the estimation of counterfactual probabilities, which are essential for computing measures of fairness. The research also addresses the problem of limited data by introducing a method that combines causal representation learning and generative adversarial networks to improve the accuracy of counterfactual probability estimation. The proposed method is tested on a variety of datasets, including simulated data and real-world data from the Adult and Dutch Census Bureau. The results show that the method can effectively estimate counterfactual probabilities and achieve fair classification outcomes. The paper concludes by discussing the future research directions and potential applications of causal representation learning in fairness analysis.

The processing of radio telescope data is becoming more feasible on local computers due to advancements in computing power, a significant factor in the development of next-generation radio telescopes. This paper introduces an open-source software solution for 21 cm hydrogen data processing, a tool that can be utilized on both 21 cm hydrogen and line emission data from radio telescopes. This software addresses the challenge of generating high-quality 21 cm hydrogen maps from large volumes of data captured by large radio telescopes, thanks to the advancement of volumetric processing capabilities. This paper presents a detailed analysis of the processing pipeline and its underlying concepts.

A new field known as metaphotonics utilizes optically-manipulated electromagnetic fields that naturally coexist with light waves. The optically-driven electric and magnetic resonances can be represented by a set of coupled Maxwell-Schrödinger equations, which simultaneously govern the behavior of classical electromagnetic fields and quantum-like probability amplitudes. The addition of a Schrodinger-like equation to the Maxwell equations enables the integration of electric and magnetic resonances, leading to the enhancement of light-matter interactions. The application of this approach in a nanophotonic cavity has demonstrated a significant boost in the coherence of electric and magnetic resonances, thereby enhancing the strength of optical forces and the efficiency of light harvesting. The efficiency of this system is further improved by tuning the magnetic resonance to compensate for the Gyrotropic effect, resulting in the efficiency of angular momentum transfer reaching 99%. The incorporation of a Schrödinger-like equation into the classical Maxwell equations enables the unification of optical manipulation and quantum control.

The effectiveness of a movie is often measured by its box office earnings, 
which are influenced by various factors, including a director's and 
actor's reputation. This study seeks to establish a reliable system for 
evaluating a director's and a star's impact on a movie's commercial success. 
To achieve this, a two-step process is proposed. Firstly, a metric for 
predicting a movie's box office performance based on its cast and crew is 
developed. This is done by using a method that assigns importance to each 
individual, known as a Micro-KG, by integrating information about a 
director's, a star's, and a movie's relationships. This is done by using 
values derived from two methods, which are based on the importance of each 
individual within their respective network. This study's results show that 
a KG-based approach can accurately predict a movie's box office performance, 
outperforming a method that uses various forms of a director's, a star's, 
and a movie's relationships. This study's results also reveal that a KG-based 
approach can accurately identify a director's and a star's impact on a 
movie's box office performance.

This paper employs linear stability analysis to investigate the influence of secondary and tertiary control on the stability properties of power grids. The analysis relies on a linearized model of an oscillating transmission line, which is influenced by inverter-based loads and generation units with droop and virtual inertia control. The results indicate that secondary frequency control has no impact on the eigenvalues of the system, and thus does not affect small-signal stability. In contrast, tertiary control can have a substantial impact on the dynamics of the network, including oscillations and transient stability, especially in networks with a high inductance-to-voltage ratio. The results are validated through numerical simulations. The study also explores the influence of control parameters on the location of the eigenvalues in the complex plane, which in turn affects the transient stability of the network. The analysis reveals that the presence of multiple areas in the network can lead to complex interactions between control parameters and eigenvalues, which in turn affects the stability of the network.

Cyber-physical systems, which integrate physical and computational processes, are now being developed with network capabilities, giving rise to connected systems that are subject to varying levels of disruption, including natural events and targeted cyber attacks. To address these challenges, a two-tier framework has been developed, consisting of an underlying network layer that manages connectivity and communication, and an application layer that oversees interactions between multiple users and services. This paper focuses on designing and implementing protocols for both layers to address disruptions and resource constraints. Specifically, a cross-layer approach is explored to address issues related to connectivity, such as network partitioning, and a matching protocol is developed to establish and maintain user associations. Additionally, a resource allocation protocol is presented to distribute resources among users based on their requirements and available network conditions.

Blazars, a type of active galactic nucleus, have their emission origins in the vicinity of a relativistic jet. Studying the polarization of UV, X-ray, and gamma-ray emissions from these objects can provide insight into their complex astrophysical environments. To gain this understanding, a simulation of jet emission from blazars is proposed, which will be based on existing models of active galactic nuclei. The focus of the jet emission simulation will be on the inverse Compton process, where jet electrons upscatter external photon fields to produce gamma-rays. By simulating the coherent Synchrotron Self-Compton emission polarization, the research will also explore the effects of polarization on blazar emissions. The code developed for this purpose, named blazersim, will be made available to the astrophysics community.

The nature of hessian matrices in disordered spin glass landscapes, characterized by randomly disordered spin glass structures, has been investigated. These matrices, essential for understanding the complexity of the landscape, exhibit distinct properties based on the number of hessians analyzed together. Our findings reveal that hessian matrices from one-step and many-step replica-symmetry broken landscapes have markedly different characteristics. Notably, in one-step broken landscapes, their distribution is symmetric and their second moment is twice the value of the fourth root mean square, whereas this symmetry is absent in many-step broken structures. These observations, supported by numerical analysis of spin glass models and analytically proven for simple glass models, provide crucial insights into the representation of spin glass landscapes by hessian matrices.

Alternative algorithms for inferring the underlying state from a sample set,
as opposed to maximum likelihood estimation,
have been scrutinized and evaluated for their performance.
In the context of three-state systems with uniform overlap,
our analysis reveals that online methods yield significantly worse outcomes.
Conversely, for systems exhibiting exponentially decaying overlap,
both online and batch methods deliver comparable results.
Consequently, the proposed methods appear to be more susceptible to noise.

A method is demonstrated to utilize the mass spectrum of light mesons to establish a natural model for QCD light baryon masses, which is then applied to calculating the light baryon mass spectra. Crucially, this approach is entirely independent. Notably, this reevaluation of the baryon mass spectra yields a significantly reduced residual mass compared to traditional constituent quark mass models.

The meridional circulation in the sun's convection zone is a key factor in the sun's dynamo, ultimately causing the sun's magnetic cycle, with its speed estimated at a few meters per second in the sun's mid-latitudes. Investigating the sun's meridional circulation is a significant scientific challenge, with acoustic wave reflections offering a potential method of measurement. This study uses three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to analyze sun-like meridional circulation and its effect on acoustic wave propagation, revealing that the flow causes a delay in wave travel times that increases with the difference between the local sound speed and the flow velocity. This delay is investigated using synthetic wave data and linear regression analysis, revealing a correlation between the derived flow velocity and the actual meridional circulation in the test simulations. This correlation is found to be robust, even in the presence of solar noise and active regions, suggesting that the linear regression method can accurately measure the sun's meridional circulation using time-dependent helioseismic data.

The presence of a magnetic field in the early universe significantly alters the behavior of gravitational waves, increasing their amplitude and potentially boosting detection chances. To explore this, the paper examines the implications of detecting a magnetic field through gravitational wave observations, taking into account various scenarios of the early universe's evolution. Observations by the LIGO and Virgo colliders place early universe magnetic field limits at frequencies of 10^4-10^8 Hz, indicating the amplitude of the gravitational wave spectrum can reach 10^-46, provided detection occurs within 10^8 years.

The four-dimensional (4D) light field (LF) image comprises multiple sub-images captured from distinct viewpoints, and can be represented as a 2D image along with an extra channel that contains disparity information. Leveraging this inherent data, our proposed two-stage differential compression framework, called TSC4D, first encodes the disparity, and then uses a differential model to compress the LF images. The framework consists of two interconnected modules: the disparity-aided image module, which generates an image-like representation from the disparity, and the latent code module, which encodes both the original and transformed LF images. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in compressing 4D LF images, and comparisons with state-of-the-art two-dimensional LF compressions reveal its superiority in terms of bit rate and visual quality.

We introduce a novel semi-interactive approach to cross-lingual information retrieval, leveraging a large language model to analyze user input queries and identify any language discrepancies. This is followed by a cross-lingual query rewriting stage, where the query is translated into a target language by aligning the query structure. Next, a search is conducted within the target-language document base. Finally, a filter is applied to the retrieved results, which are in the target language, to identify documents that match the original user query. This four-step process enhances retrieval accuracy by 3.3 points on average, as compared to non-interactive methods, by expanding the search space while maintaining query structure and relevance.

This research introduces a novel approach to tackle the "curse of dimensionality" in Bayesian spatial models by leveraging demographic data with high-resolution spatial variations. The proposed framework integrates the benefits of spatial modeling with Gaussian processes and variational inference, enabling the analysis of data with detailed spatial structures. Utilizing the stochastic nature of Gaussian processes, the method condenses the spatial dimensions into a minimal set of latent variables, thereby improving the efficiency of Bayesian spatial modeling. The efficacy of the variational Gaussian process model is evaluated through its application to the analysis of German population data across two spatial resolutions, highlighting the importance of fine-grained spatial granularity in spatial demographic analysis. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant reduction in computational time while maintaining comparable performance to a full spatial model, with an optimal latent space dimension of 100. The proposed variational Gaussian process model is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/GeorgiosKontoyiannis/demographic-analysis.

This paper introduces a quantum memory betting model that incorporates previous outcomes into the probability distribution of the next event. By accounting for history, players can make more informed decisions, with the model's capacity to remember past events being quantified by the parameter $\alpha$. In the classical scenario, players can only bet fractions of their capital, whereas quantum players can utilize superposition, entanglement, and interference to engage in "quantum gambling." Our analysis indicates that in the classical setting, an optimal gambling strategy involves betting 50% of one's capital, whereas in the quantum domain, optimal betting depends on the level of memory the player employs. Quantum memory enables the implementation of a martingale strategy, with the model's characteristics being defined by the parameter $\alpha$. When the player has full memory, the optimal strategy involves betting 100%, whereas for any finite memory level, the optimal betting amount is less than 100%. Furthermore, for the quantum memory model, the optimal betting amount is a function of $\alpha$ and is given by the expression $\beta = \frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1}$. Our model also demonstrates that the average capital growth rate is maximized at $\alpha=1$, with the maximum growth rate being $\ln 2$. Additionally, for any $\alpha<1$, the maximum capital growth rate is lower than the classical limit, with the model's first-order expansion showing that the maximum growth rate is approximately $\ln

To assess the accuracy of various computational methods, we computed the band structure and band gaps of 2D semiconductors, comparing results from density functional theory, GW calculations, and advanced corrections to density functional theory. Our findings indicate that GW calculations yield the most accurate quasiparticle energy, albeit at a higher computational cost than other methods. Notably, GW calculations show the least deviation from experimental band gaps, while the accuracy of GW calculations can be improved by incorporating advanced corrections to density functional theory, which offer a more favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider searches for the rare Sigma-plus to proton and Kaon-plus decay process using proton-proton collision data collected in 2015. Data with an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb^-1 were analyzed using a kinematic fit. No evidence of the Sigma-plus was found and upper limits on its decay width were set at 1.1 and 1.4 times 10^-25 Gev, under different assumptions about the Kaon-plus mass.

The mid-plane of a protoplanetary disk is home to a turbulent layer that transitions into a more active photoionized region near the disk's surface.  Using 21-cm data from the Mopra telescope, we studied the turbulent structure of the disk surrounding the star TWA 11410B.  We found that the disk exhibits a transition from a dense, turbulent mid-plane to a more active upper layer.  We observed that the disk's turbulent characteristics change with distance from the star, with higher turbulence and velocity differences at the outer disk regions.  We found that the disk's turbulent characteristics can be described by a model that takes into account the effects of ionized ions and neutral molecules.  We propose that the disk's turbulent characteristics are due to the presence of a dense molecular core that is surrounded by a more active photoionized region.

We have developed a method to determine the optimal atmospheric dispersion corrector design by evaluating the performance of various models, using the GAIA model as a benchmark for the Earth's atmosphere. Our research indicates that the ADCAD v2 model overestimates atmospheric dispersion in the blue range, suggesting it should be avoided in ADC designs. We have created a new model, the CDM2021, which offers significant improvements over existing models, particularly for the blue range. The CDM2021 model is a versatile tool that can be applied to any telescope, making it an essential resource for the astronomical community.

The conventional fully connected neural network, with its inherent symmetry and parameter sharing, excels at capturing intricate patterns within high-dimensional data. However, the stochastic Bayesian neural network, though offering more robust uncertainty quantification, often falls short in adapting to complex input variable relationships. In response, we present a novel Bayesian neural network with Horseshoe prior, which significantly enhances the adaptability of neural networks to intricate input dependencies. This new framework, denoted as BNN-H, boasts a faster convergence rate and superior performance compared to its fully connected counterpart, particularly in feature selection tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate a notable improvement in prediction accuracy across a range of regression and classification problems.

In this paper, we draw connections between type spaces in continuous logic, abelian groups duality, dual functors, and their application in dualizing the category of countable abelian groups with Bochner duality. We also explore how these concepts are linked to dualizing the category of countable groups under Bochner duality.

This paper's primary goal is to explore the integration of ethical considerations into the design of machine learning systems. It delves into the connections between fairness metrics, federated learning, and the intersection of fairness metrics and differential privacy. The paper's contributions include a review of the three selected areas, highlighting how they address the 'oppression' and'stereotyping' ethical issues, as well as the limited data and privacy concerns. Furthermore, it presents an ethical framework that classifies the three areas based on their relevance to specific ethical issues, data availability, and the trade-offs between privacy and accuracy.

A future collider with high sensitivity could effectively detect the $Z'$ boson resonance, which is crucial for understanding dark matter. Researchers examined how this resonance influences both dark matter's relic abundance and search strategies. In both scenarios, the parameter space for a $Z'$ boson with dark matter is more likely to be observed than in a scenario without the $Z'$ boson, as the parameter space is more constrained. Moreover, if the $Z'$ boson is within a mass range of 1 to 3 TeV, the resonance search will dominate over the dark matter search, as the parameter space is more likely to be within this mass range.

This paper explores the application of deep unsupervised learning to wireless communication systems, using a specific scenario as an example: optimizing antenna placement and signal processing in a smart reflective surface-assisted system. The authors demonstrate that leveraging unsupervised learning yields significant advantages in terms of performance and computational efficiency compared to a stochastic approach, such as a genetic algorithm. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of the two methods reveals that the unsupervised learning method is more computationally efficient.

To assess the strength of beta decays in neutron-rich nuclei, we employed a quasi-particle random phase approximation calculation. By examining the influence of nuclear configurations on this strength, we analyzed beta-strength distributions for two sets of nuclei with similar neutron numbers but different proton counts and those possessing similar proton counts but fewer shared configurations. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of a few low-lying parent and daughter states on the log ft values, analyzing their distribution across the full strength continuum, while also considering the role of a pairing gap in determining the full beta-strength distribution.

We examine a model where dark matter is comprised of stable vector and scalar particles that emerge from a $U(1)$ extension of the Standard Model and interact with leptons and right-handed neutrinos via a dynamic coupling. The dark matter's density in the universe is determined by the introduction of singlet scalars that also facilitate a connection between the dark sector and right-handed neutrinos. Additionally, the model's scalar sector is constrained by experimental data from the LHC and direct detection experiments. We also investigate the conditions under which dark matter is in thermal equilibrium with the photon-baryon fluid, allowing its presence to be detected through observations of large-scale structure. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between dark matter's density, right-handed neutrino masses, and cosmic observations of baryon density and neutrino masses.

This paper introduces a novel learning-based control strategy that leverages image data from a fixed camera to determine optimal joint angles, outperforming reinforcement learning in data-scarce environments. By establishing a mapping between observed images and joint angles, the method capitalizes on diverse visual perspectives to inform the control process. In the human-inspired xArm arm study, the proposed strategy surpasses reinforcement learning and PID controllers, particularly when data is limited. Moreover, the method exhibits greater robustness to system uncertainties compared to reinforcement learning.

The higher-spin symmetry in Toda conformal field theories is preserved and demonstrated through the satisfaction of spin-three Ward identities, which were previously calculated. This serves as a validation of the higher-spin symmetry in these theories. Additionally, the result has the potential to provide insight into the higher-spin gravity on Anti-de Sitter space.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the relation network architecture in enhancing the performance of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) across a range of image generation tasks. To achieve this, we fine-tune the standard GAN by incorporating a relation network that links the generators and discriminators within a fully adversarial framework. Our approach yields superior results on image synthesis, achieving higher Image Quality Score (IQS) on FashionMNIST, higher Frechet Inception Distance (FID) on CIFAR10, and better structural similarity through Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) on Stacking-Satellite image super-resolution. Additionally, we introduce a novel architecture known as Double GAN, which incorporates relation networks into the double GAN model.

We present a novel method for twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) that resolves its inherent ambiguity by exploiting the phase difference between reference frames of two sources. This approach enables a comparison of the relative phases and ultimately overcomes the phase uncertainty that plagues TF-QKD systems. Notably, our method does not necessitate the deployment of a dedicated optical clock or any additional hardware. Furthermore, it can be adapted to other TF-QKD protocols that rely on the preservation of quantum states.

A new class of Toeplitz operators is introduced, specifically on the $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces and their closed subspaces. First, we investigate how these operators behave when acting on a subspaces before determining under what conditions they are compact, based on the norms of the symbols within unit balls of $p$ for these spaces.

This study presents an efficient method for utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations to enhance object detectors without the need for time-consuming manual verification. We introduce a novel weak supervision approach that integrates a detection model with a simple rule-based image manipulation method to generate consistent images with adjusted pseudo bounding-boxes. These boxes are then used to establish a correlation between the image features and the boxes, allowing for the refinement of the object detector. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to tasks such as image classification and object detection, showcasing its ability to enhance model performance using a variety of models, including the widely-used ResNet and the detection models Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet, on diverse datasets such as MS COCO and PASCAL VOC.
